question: Our squads get handed tiny tickets like "tweak this button". How do I describe how far up the ladder of responsibility a squad's remit reaches, from chores to an entire product?
text:
To describe how far up the ladder of responsibility a squad's remit reaches, your sources—specifically the Org Topologies framework—provide a structured model called the Scope of Work Mandate (the vertical axis of strategic organizational design)[1][2].
This framework defines five vertical levels of responsibility that map a squad's remit from performing minor chores up to owning an entire product or business domain:
1. The 5 Levels of the Work Mandate Ladder
Tasks Focus (The Chores Level): The squad operates on fine-grained, narrow task inputs (e.g., "tweak this button" or "sketch a wireframe")[3]. The squad acts as a Doing Archetype, relying on external planners, managers, or coordinators to define, decompose, and dispatch the work[3][4][5].
Capabilities Focus (The Feature Level): The squad owns a full capability or feature set within a product or service (e.g., a search engine team or claims-processing team)[3]. They deliver functional components predictably, but their scope is restricted to their specific capability silo[3][6].
Partial-Business Focus (The Sub-Product / Vertical Level): The squad operates within a distinct business vertical or profit center (e.g., Uber Ride vs. Uber Eats)[7]. Teams at this level collaborate closely across boundaries because they are held accountable for real business outcomes and customer value rather than just output[7][8].
Whole-Business Focus (The Entire Product Level): Squads collaborate on whole-business problems, overall product direction, and customer value without internal domain silos[9][10]. They function as Driving Archetypes, uniting vision, discovery, and execution into a single self-steering unit[10][11].
Unbounded Focus (The Strategic Exploration Level): Squads have the mandate to explore undiscovered customer needs and unknown markets, pivoting freely to build brand-new value streams[9].
2. Organizational Topologies: How Squad Remit Defines the Culture
Org Topologies groups these levels into three broader Topologies to diagnose how an organization assigns authority:
Resource Topology (Directing + Doing): Squads are treated as resource pools executing task-level tickets assigned by directing roles whose primary goal is 100% resource utilization[12][13][14].
Delivery Topology (Directing + Delivering): Squads are cross-functional "feature factories" optimized for shipping complete features quickly, though high-level product strategy and discovery remain managed from above[6][15].
Adaptive Topology (Driving): Squads own both the discovery and delivery of whole-product solutions, adapting their direction continuously based on real customer outcomes[11][16][17].
3. Complementary Product & Agile Perspective
In Scrum and product management practices, elevating a squad up this ladder requires shifting from managing low-level work items to giving the squad shared accountability for a Product Goal and a single Product Backlog[18][19][20]. Leadership sets the overarching problem and goal, leaving room for the squad to leverage their expertise to figure out the "how" and deliver usable increments of value[19][21][22].
💡 Would you like to map your squad's current setup against these levels to identify what dependencies or skill gaps are keeping them stuck at the task level?

What's new in the 2025 Edition
The Org Topologies Map Language of Org Design
An archetype is a common pattern for how an organizational  unit is structured and operates, such as a cross-​functional  team that delivers end-​to-​end. Each of the 16 archetypes on  the OT map has distinct characteristics. They have short names  ("CAPS-1", "WHOLE-3",...), which creates a common org design  language, enabling change agents to accurately describe both  the current state and the desired future state of their  organization with shared understanding.

5. Unbounded.  An Expanding Unit learns whatever they need to get the job  done. In contrast, Unbounded Units have the mandate to learn anything for  unbounded exploration. This may seem unusual today, but with AI traditional  limitations vanish, so who knows where future groups can go?

Skills Mandate
Vertical Dimension of Org Design: Work Mandate The Vertical Axis
Whereas the horizontal axis is the scope of skills mandate,  the vertical represents the scope of work mandate given to  organizational units. That determines how units collaborate,  learn, and share work. The higher a unit is on the map, the  bigger is its field of play. At the highest levels, the scope of  work of different units overlaps, motivating them to learn to  co-​own and work as one super unit – “Team-​of-​Teams”.

3.chunk:
PARTIAL  BUSINESS
WHOLE  BUSINESS
From Bottom to top:
1. Tasks Focus: Units work on the narrowest scope of work. Example: A Sous-​Chef  preparing ingredients, or a visual designer sketching a wireframe. As input, they  receive fine-​grained tasks that match their expertise (“chop onions”, “design  graphic”). It’s an org design decision to limit their mandate, even though they may  be capable of learning and doing more.
2. Capabilities Focus: Units work on a full “capability” within a product or service.  Example: Insurance Claims-​Processing Group. For products, a capability is often  called a feature or function. For services, it’s also called a service element. The unit  name usually signals the capability: Surgical Team, Engine Team, Web Search Team,  and so on. Common consequences include silo thinking and local optimizations.

4.chunk:
So, an archetype can be output or outcome-​oriented. For an organizational unit to deliver outcomes, it  needs to work in a higher-​level business context, as seen on the OT map.
Complete  Archetypes
Outcome Archetypes
Output Archetypes
Incomplete  Archetypes
Four Archetype Groups Directing Archetypes
This quadrant represents directing archetypes that oversee the  higher scope of work and lack the capabilities to create customer  value. They design, coordinate, and essentially speculate on the  value by making plans and writing specs to be handed off to other  archetypes that can turn concepts into cash. Example: The  Project Manager is responsible for planning and allocating  resources to meet a project’s deadline but does not participate in  the actual creation of value.

5.chunk:
Doing Archetypes
People working in this quadrant of doing archetypes cannot  independently see “the whole” and cannot create end-​to-​end  customer value. They need to rely on external planners and  coordinators (directing archetypes), and other doing-​archetype  units (other limited specialists) to deliver value. Example: The  Sous-​Chef in a restaurant who reports to the Head Chef and has  many tactical responsibilities. 
Delivering Archetypes
This quadrant of delivering archetypes represents work units  (people, groups, teams, AI agents) capable of delivering value but  only within a narrow scope of work. Because of that, these  archetypes become siloed and may deliver the ‘wrong’ value. They  lack the big picture and flexibility to change direction dramatically  and must rely on directive archetypes for value delivery. Example:  The Search Team in an E-​Commerce software platform.

6.chunk:
However, in order to streamline delivery, discovery must  remain separated in space and time. Similar to the Resource  Topology, Directing Archetypes emphasize up-​front analysis  to supply the work, and they may direct an “analysis Doing  unit” to discover and then write “the specs”, or they may  create them themselves. 
Keeping the teams ‘fast’ and constantly ‘efficient’ in  producing the outputs is only possible when the teams in the  Delivery Archetypes are permanently fixed to a narrow work  scope—​an internal component or a specific set of  capabilities. The other side of this coin is that they cannot  easily switch contexts. By the intentions of this org design,  teams lack the work mandate to engage with the “big  picture” but are allowed to expand their skill set becoming  more and more efficient within their narrow area of expertise.

7.chunk: 3. Partial-​Business Focus: Units work on a particular business vertical, clearly  separated from the other areas. Example: Uber Ride versus Uber Eats, two separate  profit centers within a single company. A key characteristic of partial-​business units  (e.g. all Teams within Uber Ride) is cross-​team collaboration and learning because  they are closely involved in business success or failure and so care about outcomes.  The need for close collaboration between teams at this level usually leads to  organizational simplification.

8.chunk:
One consequence of an org design with complete archetypes is that they can become independently  operating silos. Whether that’s a virtue or vice depends.
Output versus Outcome Archetypes
There is a well-​known management principle of maximizing outcomes while minimizing outputs.
Outputs—​such as number of surgeries, amount of software features, number of completed design  documents, or percentage of closed insurance claims—​are relatively straightforward leading metrics.  However, more output does not mean more outcomes. In fact, more output usually means more cost or  investment, which can lower profit (an outcome). Investing to increase outcomes (healthy people, profit) is  justified; ‘investing’ to increase output is suspect.

9.chunk:
4. Whole-​Business Focus: Units work and collaborate on whole-​business problems  and customer value. Example: Two-​person Instagram-​like startup. There is no  permanent separation inside the unit, such as business verticals, sub-​products, or  alike. At a larger scale, Teams may have a short-​term focus but are not stuck there.
5. Unbounded: This level refers to a state where units go where they want to explore  new ideas to satisfy undiscovered customer needs, possibly from unknown markets.  And they learn whatever they need. Example: A startup, such as a failing games  company who kept pivoting until they found a product that succeeded, in their  case, the collaboration tool Slack.

10.chunk:
Driving Archetypes
This is not ‘driving’ others. Imagine a car with passengers, any one of  whom can drive, who together decide where they want to go, drive and  arrive, and then go on. These driving archetypes are capable of  understanding, creating, and delivering customer value in its broadest  sense. That's where directing, doing, and delivering come together.  These archetypes can grasp the concept of business objectives or end-​ to-​end customer journeys and deliver upon them jointly thanks to an  overlapping, shared scope of work and a broad skills mandate. Example:  A three-​person startup or five teams within a Team-​of-​Teams.

11.chunk:
DIRECTING
DELIVERING
Delivery Topology: Directing + Delivering
Adaptive Topology The Adaptive Topology merges “directing, doing, and  delivering” into one holistic unit within the Driving archetypes,  where humans, AI agents, and robots collaborate on complex  problems in an adaptive way, and the group explores and  drives themselves in their ‘car’. The goal of this topology is  adaptiveness (easy, cheap change based on learning) and  customer-​centricity to discover and deliver customer delight.

12.chunk:
Resource Topology There are three common Org Topologies to know, starting  with: The Resource Topology—​a topology characterized by  frozen functional archetypes specialized in one domain. Its  purpose is to ensure that each unit is 100% utilized (i.e.  resource utilization). It is seen in “resource management”  approaches where “resource managers” (or project  managers) are responsible for planning and monitoring  resource allocation and utilization.
In this topology, the value-​creation work takes place among  the Doing Archetypes in the lower left quadrant. However,  none of these can independently produce end-​to-​end  customer value. They depend on each other due to narrow  specialization. Additionally, they lack a clear and holistic  understanding of customer value, as their work mandate  focuses solely on specific tasks or capabilities.

13.chunk: The Directing Archetypes in the upper left quadrant treat  the Doing Archetypes as “resources,” matching skill demand  with skill supply. The Delivery Archetypes do not participate  in high-​level discovery due to ‘efficiency’ justifications.  Consequently, analysis in the form of detailed specifications  (a film Wardrobe Breakdown, a software Requirement Spec)  are handed over for implementation. This topology requires  traditional project management with significant upfront  planning and estimation, and frequent monitoring and  replanning in cases of high variability.

14.chunk: In the example mapping on the right, we see a Directing  Archetype (the Product Manager at WHOLE-1), who  oversees the whole business and passes product  development ideas to the Doing Archetypes. This is where  we see a functional department, where project managers  understand product capabilities (CAPS-1). Their job is to  break them into tasks for the developers. They decompose,  plan, dispatch and monitor the work. Some of the  developers work as cross-​functional teams (TASKS-2),  others are in functional resource pools (TASKS-1). This  example is a Resource Topology, whose goal is maximizing  resource utilization. It produces organizational capabilities  like predictability and specialization, making it well-​suited  for environments with a low need for product discovery, and  where slow delivery of value is not a problem.

15.chunk:
DIRECT﻿ING 
DOING
Resource Topology: Directing + Doing
Delivery Topology Compared to the Resource Topology, this topology upgrades  delivery units to have fast flow by removing dependencies.  Structurally, this typically involves forming complete cross-​ functional teams, and facilitating a smoother path to  “completely done” work. In some domains, this topology is  called a “Feature Factory” since Delivery units can provide a  near-​endless stream of features. Note a strong focus on  outputs and local efficiency.

16.chunk:
The boundaries between teams are structurally removed and  replaced by larger constructs—​such as a Team-​of-​Teams—​ where organizational units work closely together across the  entire business (“Uber”) or a partial business domain (“Uber  Eats”).
“Synchronicity of work” is a unique emergent quality of this  topology: in contrast to the other two topologies where the  Doing and Delivering archetypes own a narrow scope of work,  here in the Adaptive Topology, the Driving archetype allows all  parties to work in unison.

17.chunk:
Inside the Driving archetypes of the Adaptive Topology,  individuals (human and AI) form a network and create a  learning organization that shares objectives and learns to  operate as one. We refer to the archetypes in this topology as  Elevated to distinguish them from the Resource and Delivery  topologies. Its core features include:
Broad scope of capabilities and work. Synchronous work, coordinated by those performing the  work. Continuous learning both vertically (across the scope of  work) and horizontally (across the scope of skills), making  it cheap and easy to switch strategic direction.

Scrum Team
The fundamental unit of Scrum is a small team of people, a Scrum Team. The Scrum Team consists of
one Scrum Master, one Product Owner, and Developers. Within a Scrum Team, there are no sub-teams
or hierarchies. It is a cohesive unit of professionals focused on one objective at a time, the Product Goal.
Scrum Teams are cross-functional, meaning the members have all the skills necessary to create value
each Sprint. They are also self-managing, meaning they internally decide who does what, when, and

19.chunk:
Product Owner
The Product Owner is accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of
the Scrum Team. How this is done may vary widely across organizations, Scrum Teams, and individuals.
6
The Product Owner is also accountable for effective Product Backlog management, which includes:
• Developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal;
• Creating and clearly communicating Product Backlog items;
• Ordering Product Backlog items; and,
• Ensuring that the Product Backlog is transparent, visible and understood.

20.chunk:
Commitment: Product Goal
The Product Goal describes a future state of the product which can serve as a target for the Scrum Team
to plan against. The Product Goal is in the Product Backlog. The rest of the Product Backlog emerges to
define “what” will fulfill the Product Goal.
A product is a vehicle to deliver value. It has a clear boundary, known stakeholders, well-defined
users or customers. A product could be a service, a physical product, or something more abstract.
The Product Goal is the long-term objective for the Scrum Team. They must fulfill (or abandon) one

22.chunk:
Topic Three: How will the chosen work get done?
For each selected Product Backlog item, the Developers plan the work necessary to create an Increment
that meets the Definition of Done. This is often done by decomposing Product Backlog items into
smaller work items of one day or less. How this is done is at the sole discretion of the Developers. No
one else tells them how to turn Product Backlog items into Increments of value.
